title: Show up in a good way – On Zen and Solidarity with Indigenous Water Protectors
speaker: Ben Connelly
summary: The talk's main teaching is that showing up in a good way means approaching each moment with intentionality, care, and compassion for all beings. This involves being fully present and engaged, without judgment or control, and recognizing our interconnectedness with others and the environment. By embracing this mindset, we can cultivate freedom from frustration and find empowerment in our choices and actions, rather than trying to control external events.

sentences.text: Good morning and thank you for coming to our Sunday Zen life.
I apologize for the good weather because it looks like everybody's out having fun.
So great apologies to Ben, who will give our dharma talk today.
It is such an incredible pleasure to have the renowned writer and Zen priest and all-around wonderful guy to give dharma talk to us.

I just found out that he will be publishing a new book, and it's a study guide about Vasubandhu, and I'm really looking forward to it because this commentary is like the first one that made any sense to me, so I'm looking forward to the sequel.
You all recognize this book, which is what we worked with for our last practice period and the practice period last year, so that was really wonderful.
Me, as an almost like mindfulness teacher, even though I don't practice it, this was a really incredible book, so it really went beyond mere mindfulness to touching the heart.
Thank you so much, Ben, for sharing your morning with us, and again, low numbers, but we are totally here.
We are totally here.
Yeah, already complete, so I'm just glad to be with those of you I'm with.
It's nice to see you.
Thanks so much for having me here.
Chris has fond memories of visiting to teach at Red Cedar a few years ago when I was doing some teaching travels, and it's a lot easier to do teaching travels these days.
So I push a button and zoom.
Anyway, I'm in Minnesota; it's quite beautiful here.
We've had a late spring, and so everything's blooming all at once, but yeah, it's just wonderful.
I'll give you a talk about how great it is to be outside, and then maybe you can go be outside.
But you know, inside and outside are just ideas anyway.
I'm just going to jump in because I have prepared remarks.
I think I called this talk something like "Show up in a good way: Lessons from following indigenous water protectors."

I'm recalling an instance last summer, a little later, just about maybe eleven months ago, and I was at a prayer circle as part of a multi-day event in northern Minnesota called the Treaty People Gathering, which was a gathering of several thousand people to do training and how nonviolent direct action to oppose the construction of the Line Three pipeline that runs through a bunch of Anishinaabe wetlands across something like a dozen rivers across the Mississippi River at three places near its headwaters.
And, spoiler alert, the pipeline is built and oil is running through it—tar sands oil from Canada is running through that pipeline—but we put a lot of effort into opposing that pipeline.
One of the things was this big multi-day nonviolent direct action event that was led predominantly by indigenous women, indigenous leaders, and other people as well.
On the day after the trainings, we had a prayer gathering, a multi-faith prayer gathering before we were going to go out on the highway and engage in nonviolent direct action.
It was very beautiful; there were all kinds of people there, all different religions represented: Hindus, Buddhists, Christians, Jews, Muslims, indigenous people.
One of the speakers in the circle was Great Grandmother Mary Lions, who is an Anishinaabe woman who does a lot of water protector activities and a lot of indigenous rights advocacy.
She tends to travel with a contingent of her female relatives, so there would be like three generations of Anishinaabe women, all wearing these matching traditional dresses that come with her.
She stands in the front and delivers this message, and her family is with her; she's just a powerful figure.
She's completely hilarious, and telling someone someone is funny is not that exciting, but it's true; she's really funny, but she's also willing to be completely unflinching.

In this talk at this prayer circle, which was predominantly attended by people who are not indigenous, she talked very clearly about the brutal impacts on her family and on the people from her Anishinaabe community by white settlers and their descendants, so people like me.

She talked about the really negative impacts of the pipeline construction, which has been opposed by a large number of Anishinaabe people, both on the land and on their livelihood and on their spiritual lives.

Fossil fuel projects tend to be accompanied by sex trafficking, and frequently with pipelines, it's of indigenous women, so you see a pattern of murdered and missing indigenous women following fossil fuel projects, which she talked about in very stark terms.

And of course, in case it's not obvious, there are many, many people who are knowledgeable about climate change; we're seeing any investment in large-scale fossil fuel infrastructure projects is really counterproductive.
She just laid this out, and it was like, you know, and I'm just standing there in my robe behind her, just like, wow, the heat is on.
The heat is on for this white Zen priest.
Towards the end, or right at the end of her offering, she said, "All right, I'm glad you're here, and I hope you will show up in a good way."

I gather that it may be in many indigenous North American cultures, maybe just an Anishinaabe thing, but the phrase "show up in a good way" is kind of a stock spiritual phrase, you know, like "freeing all beings" for Soto Zen Buddhism, but anyway, "show up in a good way."
I was like, well, that sounds like a good idea; I'm up for trying that.
This idea of showing up in a good way aligns really deeply with Buddhist teachings.

The person who transmitted the teaching through my lineage, Category Roshi, talked a great deal about being upright about realizing you're in this moment and bringing your whole self in a dignified, noble, and liberating way—being upright, showing up in a good way.

When I talk to people about what this means, it sounds a very common valence, particularly when it comes to Buddhism, this idea of showing up in a good way really makes sense because she didn't say, "I hope you will be successful in stopping this pipeline from being built," or, "I hope you will overcome all the police officers who are amassing down there to do God knows what to you."
And by the way, the police officers were very chill where I was, but they totally brutalized the other people at the other direct action.
Many friends of mine, I won't go into details, but it was bad.
So anyway, she didn't say, "I hope you'll win," or "I hope you'll beat the cops," or "I hope you'll stop the pipeline"; she said, "I hope you will show up in a good way."

This is a central element of Buddhist thought that runs from the earliest teachings through many different types of Buddhism, which is the primacy of intentionality and the importance of the quality with which we approach the moment.
It is important to say this isn't saying that the impact doesn't matter; it's just emphasizing that we can claim our power when we think about what we're doing and how we're doing it.

Think less about controlling and manipulating apparently external objects, which if you read Buddhist teachings, there's very little instruction about how to control and manipulate apparently external objects.

So, well, of course, you know, showing up in a good way what would that look like could mean a lot of things, but hopefully, understanding how everything is interdependent, understanding that what you do has impact, understanding the systems that you're in, and showing up because you care about everyone, you want everyone to be free and willing to give everything up so that can happen—well, that sounds great.
That sounds great.
But how often does that happen?

I guess a lot of times I could be like, "Well, I'd like to show up in a good way," but for example, while I was up there at the Treaty People Gathering, there were moments where I was like, "I'm just scared."

I've got these trainers telling me, "Well, you know, if they start tear gassing, here's what you do," and I'm like, "Well, I got tear gas last year in Minneapolis, and what I did is ran away because it's really unpleasant."

So, there's like fear, was that showing up in a good way, or I might just be like complacent, "I don't want to deal with it," or I might be like, "Judging, oh, I hate the bad people; they're really stupid and wrong, and once they get it figured out, then we'll all be okay," or whatever it is.
All those things occur in the hearts and minds of people, and that doesn't mean you can't show up in a good way.
When we feel despair, we feel fear, we feel rage, we feel shame, we feel complacency—in every one of those cases, we can show up in a good way for that feeling state itself.

And that is really, really powerful to turn and say, "Oh, I feel this way right now, not whatever my mind is telling you about the external world is absolutely true and I need to just go off on an endless line of thinking about it, but what is going on in this body and this heart, and can I show up in a good way for that?"
I went up to northern Minnesota as part of this ongoing action led by indigenous women Winona LaDuke, Tara Houska, Tanya Aboud, a bunch of folks.

Tanya Aboud and Winona LaDuke had started a place they were calling the Water Protector Welcome Center, which Winona, I don't know if you know her, she like ran for Vice President on the Green Party ticket a few years ago, probably quite a few years ago.
Anyway, she's an indigenous woman, and she's one of the leaders up there, what's going on.

She had acquired this land that was on the Mississippi, so you can walk from the encampment to the Mississippi River, which at that point is about fifty yards wide, so if you've ever seen it in New Orleans, it's like a mile across, but up near the headwaters, it's just a little; it's a pretty small river.

You can walk right down to the river and the land directly above one of the three places where the Enbridge company was going to be drilling the pipe under the river, so you can just walk to the edge of the property and look at the drill pad site.
There was all kinds of stuff that happened with this water protector camp, all kinds of spiritual rituals and protest actions.

One of the things that had happened is Winona LaDuke and Tanya Aboud had built an indigenous Anishinaabe prayer lodge right where the drill was supposed to go, and they did it before any of the drilling equipment could go in.
They have treaty-protected rights to use the land up there for hunting, fishing, gathering, and religious purposes, so they had treaty-protected rights to be there.

They were able to hold that spot because they were treaty-protected for a long time until the police decided that they didn't care about the treaty rights and they evicted them, and now the pipe is built.
They were having people up there, and we would go up there and do various things at the camp to try and be helpful.
One day I went up there, and a lot of times I'd go up with Minnesota Interfaith Power and Light.
We'd have gatherings, and we'd often gather at the river first for a prayer circle, and then we'd go and do some other stuff.
One of the times I went up there, we got there for the prayer circle.
Northern Minnesota is a beautiful, pristine place.

There is one of the largest parcels of wilderness in the lower forty-eight up by the Boundary Waters, an hour or two north of where we are, which is right by the headwaters of the Mississippi, and the river's there.
But at this time that I was there, they had the drilling equipment in.
The drilling equipment is a huge, huge machine, like a gigantic thing that's driving a pipe several feet wide that's going to go several hundred yards underground underneath the Mississippi River.
It is grinding and churning and roaring twenty-four hours a day, or was for a week or two.
I was up there at this prayer gathering, standing in a circle by the river, and there's just this roaring sound coming from about one hundred fifty yards away.
It's a beautiful, pristine nature, and they're just mechanized construction happening; there's a lot going on.
People are offering these beautiful prayers—Jewish prayers, Christian prayers, Muslim prayers—and I was like, "Oh, I can have an offering I can make."
I said, "Oh, I have an offering because we were just like, hey, I'll say something, you know, it's just people being together, making offerings."
So I recited this poem by Laywoman Chen, who is, I think, maybe an eleventh-century Chinese nun, or not a nun, she's a laywoman, Buddhist, and she wrote:
*Up on the high slopes, I see only woodcutters.
Everyone has the spirit of the knife and the axe.
How could they see the mountain flowers reflected in the water?
Glorious.
Red.*
I recited this poem, and it felt very appropriate to this kind of pristine environment that was also the site of this really intense, mechanized progress.
And then the prayers are all wrapped up, and we went back across the street and we're like, "All right, well, let's get to work."
We got stuff to do at camp.
The great thing about camp is there's always a lot of dishes to do, and as a Zen student, there's one thing I've learned how to do: I can do dishes.
So I got to wash a lot of dishes.
I feel really expert; they're like, "Wow, we've got a great expert here in our midst."
Anyway, I got to wash a lot of dishes.
But on this day, right after the prayer circle, I came back and they said, "Okay, we're going to have a work party.
Jim Northrup is going to come."
If you know a lot about northern Minnesota indigenous elders, there's a Jim Northrup who's published a lot of well-known books.
He is deceased.
His son was here just to clear it because I was like, "How can Jim Northrup be coming into camp?
Because I'm pretty sure he's not alive."
So anyway, his son came and was like, "Okay, he's going to lead a work party."
I was like, "Oh, this is cool.
Get to meet Jim Northrup's son."
Jim Northrup comes in and he says, "Hi, everybody.
Well, I need a work party.
You know, any volunteers?"
I'm like, "Yeah, a bunch of people volunteer.
Come over."
Okay, here's what we're going to do.
And he pulled out a big axe.
And he said, "We're going to go cut down a bunch of trees.
Who has the spirit of the knife and the axe now?"
So he said, "Yeah, we want to build another larger prayer lodge down by the drill pad site next to the one that Tanya and Winona made.
And we need to get like forty two-inch diameter hard maples that are about thirty feet tall.
We're going to take them down with this axe.
We're going to trim them up with loppers and with the axe and then we'll pull them out.
And then probably tomorrow we'll make the watch."
So I thought, well, this is ironic.
Here I was.
I was all pretty cool.
I'm here looking at the mountain flowers and those bad Enbridge people with their knife and the axe are making their big pipe.
And now I'm like, "All right, hand me that axe.
Let's get to work."
The tendency to want to make someone else the other is so pervasive in human consciousness.
And there are so many opportunities to see that we're in this together and that they're making that pipeline.
And I own an automobile, you know, and I will use fossil fuels for many purposes.
So we're in it together.
It's not a battle.
It's an ongoing relationship.
So anyway, I got out and I cut down some trees.
That was cool.
That's cool.
You know how it is.
I get yours and practice or like I know how to do work practice.
You just give yourself to it.
So I was like out in the woods, just find the tree, cut the tree, drag the tree, working with people.
You know, it was pretty good.
It was good.
But I realized, you know, ways through it was like, "Wow, you know, I'm pretty good at doing wholehearted activity, really doing what I'm doing with my whole being."
But it's very easy for something to be left out.
How much am I losing sight of the fact that I'm taking this tree's life?
How does this tree feel about this wholehearted activity?
So wholehearted activity is like I have to remember that wholehearted activity should include continually expanding the frame of who is included in why I'm acting.
And that doesn't mean I wouldn't cut down the trees, but it might change the quality, the way I show up, the degree to which I show up in a good way for those trees and for the activity.
So in the Genjokoan, Dogen says, "The air is life and the water is life."
Well, that's pretty cool because I've been marching up and down highways in northern Minnesota with huge signs that say water is life.
They were painted by these wonderful artists who come up to be a part of this movement to stop line three.
Oh, well, look, Dogen says water is life.
And that's what we're saying right here.
It's cool.
We're going to protect the waters.
So the air is life and the water is life.
And the context in which Dogen says this is in the Genjokoan, which is arguably sort of the key, like the most compact summation of his approach.
And the context is one where he says, "Well, it's like you have a fish swimming in the water.
It's always in the water.
It can go forever.
I mean, he doesn't isn't talking about depth and life, but he's like, in terms of its range, you could swim all over.
You could swim the ocean, just swim and swim and swim.
You never leave the water."
And you might think, "Well, there's a fish that's alive and then there's water that it is in."
And he's like, "That is not a good way to look at it.
The water is life.
The entirety of the environment is the life of the organism."
Likewise with the bird.
The bird flies in the sky.
There is no end to its range.
It can fully experience its element.
But if the bird leaves the diet, if the bird leaves the air, it will die at once.
Just recognizing that we tend to see an alienated world with sentient beings that operate in a material reality.
And this is not a helpful worldview.
It's not a helpful worldview.

Both the teachings of Dogen and the teachings of the indigenous people who are up there working so hard to care for the world that they live in is based in a realization that the life is the whole of that interdependent system.
So, you know, it's good to think about this.
You know, thinking is pretty cool, actually.
I don't know how zen you are.
Are you guys like really, really zen?
So you think thinking is a bad idea?
Well, that's an idea.
Anyway, thinking is pretty cool.
Thinking is pretty cool.
And, you know, so it can really help to think about how things are related.
To use your mind to dismantle the tendency to create a world of alienation.
But it's also possible to just make that space so that the activity of mind slows down because the way things are already is interdependence.
So you don't have to make it true by thinking about it.
So you can become more aware of it using thought, and you can be more aware of it by letting thought subside.
And so this is one of the reasons why zazen is such great value.
At the treaty people gathering, there were a lot of Buddhists there.
I decided to do a little bit of organizing.
And basically all I did was I created a Google Doc and I emailed everyone I know who I thought might be going.
And I said, "Hey, share this with everyone you think might be going.
Let's all put our names on this document so we can connect and just see who's going."
Well, it turned out there were like way more than forty Buddhists up here.
That's forty people who spent three days doing direct action, many of whom got arrested.
People will be like, "Why don't Buddhists ever engage in anything?
You're talking to different ones than I am."
Anyway, so there we were, but we would go up and of course we like to have a little quiet time.

So the days were pretty full, but a whole bunch of us would get up in the mornings and practice meditation and have a short service on the lake shore at our camp each day before the formal activities began.
And the last day that we were there, we sat down for zazen and I brought down a little something to keep my butt dry basically.
And I sat down and I looked ahead of me and there was a leatherback turtle about this big.
The scale is hard to see.
It's about eighteen inches long.
And it was about ten yards in front of me and it was busy laying eggs in a hole that it had just dug.
So, you know, I like just turned my gaze down and like, "Oh, there's a huge turtle there."
She was very diligent.
It's not easy to lay eggs, you know.
It didn't look like it was easy, but she was just doing her thing.
And then after she laid all the eggs, she got up and she started, she had back legs so she's paddling the dirt back into the hole.
And then she walked all the way around the hole and looked at it and then she sat back down there and paddle it so you get a little bit better, you know, like you'd feather your nest.
And she did that about three times and then she walked back to the lake and all that took about forty-five minutes.
She was taking her, she's not in a hurry, evidently.
I don't think she could have moved any faster if she wanted to.
Anyway, I was able to just be there with her.
Because I got up in the morning early and just said, "I'm just going to walk over there and sit there and not do anything."
And then I was able to experience a profound intimacy.
I'm not something special, just realizing that I was with the environment that I was in.
So I want to make some concluding remarks here.
Show up in a good way.
I'm into it.
I encourage you to show up in a good way.
One of the cool things about Soto Zen Buddhism is you already did.
Are you here?
You have shown up in a good way.
The Genjokoan opens with this line: *As all dharmas are Buddha Dharma, there is delusion and realization, practice and birth and death.
And there are Buddhas and sentient beings.* I'll just say that again.
*As all dharmas are Buddha Dharma, there is delusion and realization, practice and birth and death, Buddhas and sentient beings.* It goes on to say a lot of other things.
But this opening line basically says that the only grounds on which it is reasonable to say that anything exists is that it is Buddha.
The only reasonable ground on which to say anything exists is if you are saying that it is Buddha.
Now, he says some other things, too.
But that's where we start.
Or in the Fukanzazengi, he was like, "I'm going to recommend you do zazen."
He's like, "The way is originally perfect and all pervading.
How can it be contingent on practice and realization?
Well, you and I may be very special.
So we may be the only place in the universe where the way does not pervade."
But I don't think that's what he's teaching us.
I don't think you can get out of it.
I think everything is showing up and in a good way.
And this may seem paradoxical or just ridiculous.
In the simplest terms, using a Yogachara teaching, the totality of our experience right now, minus the ideas we have about it, is the truth.
And if you subtract all the ideas about it, all the things that turn it into suffering and that cause us to do things that cause suffering are absent as well.
And it's already not the things we think it is.
And we already can't control any of the things we won't think we can control.
So I know it's very weird.
But here's the thing.
There's freedom there.
There's freedom there.
If you can't control anything, well, all those frustrations go away because you're like, "Well, I'm not trying to control anything.
I'm just going to show up in a good way because I have shown up in a good way.
I'm going to show up in a good way."
Now, conventionally speaking, yeah, it takes some energy.
It takes some personal conviction to show up in a good way.
The other side of this system of thought in Buddhism is that everything we do plant seeds for what will be experienced.
So the way we show up moment to moment is our actual contribution with drawing the attention from the control of apparently external objects and focus on how we choose to act.
And this puts us in the seat where we have the most power and the most agency, which feels a lot better than feeling like, "Why can't I make stuff happen the way I want it to?"
Which you and I may feel now and again.
So I'm just grateful that we have shown up in a good way together.
And I think it would just be nice to hear other people's voices reflecting on what I've been talking about.
Sometimes when I show up, people want to ask me questions about totally unrelated things because they have read books that I wrote.
That's fine.
If you want to do that, I'm just here.
But anyway, yeah, you can ask questions or you can just save reflections or things that come to mind or whatever.
Inspire everybody or be real.
Whatever.
You can just jump in.
